summary: Specifies the conventions for using the US Government's NSA Suite B cryptography in IPsec. Because many Suite B algorithms are used elsewhere, most conventions are already given in other documents, so this profile mostly references those. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: A government wanted certain secret-code methods used for safe network connections. This explains how to use them with IPsec. It is historic now.

which ipsec suites does suite b allow
does suite b ipsec allow ikev1
subtitle: How to use the US NSA Suite B cryptography with IPsec and IKEv2, mostly by pointing at other documents.

tldr.problem: The US Government's Suite B guidelines set cryptographic algorithm policy for national security applications, and implementers needed to know how to apply them in IPsec.
tldr.mechanism: The profile requires IKEv2 and one of four UI suites from RFC 6379, with ECDSA authentication and ECDH on the P-256 or P-384 curve, at a 128-bit or 192-bit minimum level of security.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is now Historic, so it is a record of the profile rather than a current recommendation.

today: RFC 6380 is Historic, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Read it as a record of the Suite B profile for IPsec rather than a current recommendation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document specifies the conventions for using NSA Suite B Cryptography in IP Security (IPsec). Many Suite B algorithms are used in other environments, so most of the needed conventions are already defined elsewhere. The RFC references those sources and repeats some detail to help developers who choose to support Suite B.

Suite B compliant IPsec implementations MUST use IKEv2 and MUST use one of the four cryptographic user interface suites defined in RFC 6379, depending on the desired security level and security services. The suites cover options for IKEv2 and for the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP, RFC 4303).
sections.eli5: This is a rulebook that says which approved secret-code recipes to use for private network connections. Most of the details live in other books, so this one mostly points to them.

sections.title: Suite B Algorithms and Security Levels
sections.content:
Suite B requires key establishment and signatures to be based on Elliptic Curve Cryptography and encryption to use AES. It includes AES with 128 and 256 bit keys, ECDSA for digital signatures, ECDH for key exchange (both using curves with 256 and 384 bit prime moduli), and the hashes SHA-256 and SHA-384.

The two curves go by different names: P-256 (nistp256, secp256r1, IANA DH group 19) and P-384 (nistp384, secp384r1, IANA DH group 20).

Suite B has two minimum levels of security: 128 bits (minLOS_128) and 192 bits (minLOS_192). The non-signature primitives fall into two columns. At 128 bits they MUST come exclusively from Column 1 or exclusively from Column 2. At 192 bits they MUST come exclusively from Column 2.
sections.eli5: There are two strength settings, medium and strong. Each uses a matching set of lock, key-swap and fingerprint tools, and you cannot mix the sets in the strong setting.

sections.title: IKEv2 Authentication and Certificates
sections.content:
Digital signatures using ECDSA MUST be used for authentication. RFC 4754 defines ECDSA-256 (P-256 curve with SHA-256) and ECDSA-384 (P-384 curve with SHA-384).

At the 128-bit level, a system MUST use either ECDSA-256 or ECDSA-384, and one party may use one while the other uses the other. Systems MUST be able to verify ECDSA-256 and SHOULD be able to verify ECDSA-384. At the 192-bit level, both parties MUST use ECDSA-384 and MUST be able to verify it.

Other authentication methods MUST NOT be used. A relying party that receives a message signed another way MUST return an AUTHENTICATION_FAILED notification and stop processing it. Each side MUST use an X.509 certificate that complies with the Suite B certificate profile in RFC 5759 and holds an elliptic curve public key with the digital signature key usage bit set.
sections.eli5: Each side signs a note to prove who it is. Only the approved kinds of signature count, and anything else is turned away.

sections.title: Suites and Security Associations
sections.content:
The four suites from RFC 6379 are Suite-B-GCM-128, Suite-B-GMAC-128, Suite-B-GCM-256 and Suite-B-GMAC-256. They differ in algorithm strength and in whether ESP gives both confidentiality and integrity (GCM) or integrity only (GMAC). GCM suites MUST be used when both are needed; GMAC suites MUST be used only when there is no need for ESP encryption.

At the 128-bit level an initiator MUST offer one or more of the four suites, with the 128 suites listed before the 256 ones. A responder MUST support one or both 128 suites, SHOULD support the 256 ones, and MUST return a NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN notification if none of the four is offered. At the 192-bit level an initiator MUST offer Suite-B-GCM-256 or Suite-B-GMAC-256, and a responder MUST choose one of them or return the same error.
sections.eli5: Both sides swap a menu of approved options and must pick one from the list. If nothing on the menu is approved, the answer is no.

sections.title: Key Exchange and Keying Material
sections.content:
In the IKE_SA_INIT exchange, each side MUST generate an ephemeral elliptic curve key pair, on P-256 if the 256-bit random ECP group is selected and on P-384 if the 384-bit group is selected. Public keys go in the key exchange payload as in RFC 5903.

The ECDH shared secret is the x value of the common value, 256 or 384 bits for P-256 or P-384. An ephemeral private key MUST be used in exactly one key establishment and MUST be zeroized afterwards, and the shared secret MUST be zeroized immediately after use, as NIST SP800-56A requires.

With PRF-HMAC-SHA-256, the values SKEYSEED, SK_d, SK_pi and SK_pr MUST each be 256 bits; with PRF-HMAC-SHA-384 they MUST each be 384 bits. SK_ei and SK_er MUST be 128 or 256 bits when the AES key length attribute is 128 or 256.
sections.eli5: The two sides make throwaway secrets, mix them to get a shared key, and then must wipe the throwaway secrets so nobody can find them later.

sections.title: Additional Requirements
sections.content:
AH is not supported in Suite B compliant implementations. Suite B systems MUST support IKEv2 and MUST NOT use IKEv1 between a compliant initiator and responder. A system may be configured to use IKEv1 for backward compatibility, but then it is not operating in a Suite B compliant mode.

For CREATE_CHILD_SA, any Diffie-Hellman key MUST use the same random ECP group as the IKE_INIT_SA, and rekeying MUST be supported by both parties. Identification payloads MUST NOT be used for policy lookup; the authentication method MUST use an end-entity found in the certificate instead.

The administrative user interface MUST allow the operator to specify a single suite, and the implementation then offers only that suite. It MAY allow several, in which case it MUST let the operator set a preferred order. The RFC's Security Considerations section says only that it discusses security requirements throughout and inherits those of RFC 4303, RFC 4754, RFC 5759 and RFC 5996.
sections.eli5: A few extra rules close loopholes: no older, weaker systems, no shortcuts for looking up who is who, and the operator can choose which approved options are allowed.
